title: Tools for Reducing Service Time in Near-Term Quantum Networks
authors: Jake Smith, Thomas R. Beauchamp, Scarlett Gauthier, Oumayma Bouchmal, Stephanie Wehner
abstract: Architectures have been proposed to control entanglement generation in multi-user quantum networks. To allow time for local operations and classical communication at end nodes, these architectures insert fixed separations between consecutive batches of entanglement generation attempts. This reduces network utilization when attempts fail, leaving the network idle during the scheduled separation. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method to reclaim this idle time by shortening the scheduled separation between attempts while respecting hardware constraints. The method uses an analytical execution model to optimize the separation and reduce the total network service time of an application. Evaluations within the Arqon architecture show network service time reductions of up to 42 minutes (7.6%) for single applications and 16-29 minutes (26-30%) per application when co-scheduled. The approach applies broadly to quantum network architectures that share hardware between entanglement generation and local operations, and the method can be used online by network schedulers.
summary: This work introduces a novel method to optimize resource utilization in near-term quantum networks by intelligently shortening the mandatory idle time scheduled between entanglement generation attempts. By analytically modeling the scheduling process, the authors demonstrate significant reductions in total service time, especially when multiple applications share the quantum hardware. This is crucial for making quantum network services more efficient and practical.
main_problem: The paper addresses the inefficiency in near-term quantum networks caused by mandatory idle time scheduled between entanglement generation attempts.
main_result: The proposed optimization method can reduce the total network service time by up to 30% when multiple applications are co-scheduled.
method: It uses an analytical execution model, treating the scheduling problem as an optimization to shorten the scheduled separation time while maintaining required service probabilities.
model_or_system: The system is a multi-user quantum network utilizing the Arqon architecture, which generates shared entanglement for quantum information applications.
key_observables: Network service time reduction (up to 30% for co-scheduled apps), session execution speedup, and the optimized scheduled separation time.
important_parameters: Minimum separation time ($t_{minsep}$), service probability, and the degree of co-scheduling.
main_assumptions: The optimization assumes a balance between minimizing time and ensuring the target number of instances is completed with a specified service probability.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the comparison between full minimum separation and reduced separation in the scheduling process.
paper_structure: The paper identifies the scheduling limitation, proposes the analytical optimization method, applies it to the Arqon architecture, and presents quantitative results comparing reduced vs. baseline service times.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, resource-management optimization technique applicable to the scheduling overhead inherent in building and operating quantum communication infrastructure.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The ingress α is the fraction of PGA i by which the scheduled separation is shortened, giving T ′ = tminsep −αE. At α = 0 (top) the full minimum separation is kept and the network idles after an early tgen. At α > 0 (bottom) the separation shortens by αE, reclaiming idle time. A packet generated within the shaded ingress region risks a minimum separation violation (Section IV-B).

Fig. 2. Average packet generation time (solid, left axis) and PGA duration (dashed, right axis) as a function of packet generation probability ppacket for the state-of-the-art regime (left; λ = 2.22 Hz, w = 275 ms) and optimistic regime (right; λ = 10 Hz, w = 2 s). Both quantities are normalized by the window length w to enable comparison across demands with different PGA durations. Demands are labeled by their requested link count s, with z-scores z = (s −λw)/ √

Fig. 3. Probability pmv of a minimum separation violation, conditioned on successful packet generation. The surfaces are shown as a function of PGA ingress α and packet generation probability ppacket. Two configurations are compared: requested links s = 2 in the state-of-the-art regime (left; λ = 2.22 Hz, w = 275 ms, z = 1.8) and s = 10 in the optimistic regime (right; λ = 10 Hz, w = 2 s, z = −2.2). Each grid point is estimated from 104 successful trials obtained by rejection sampling. White contours are spaced at intervals of 0.1. These surfaces are computed once per physical configuration (λ, w, s) and stored as lookup tables for use by the Markov chain session model.
